verses.text: The king sent, and they gathered to him all the elders of Judah and of Jerusalem.

The king went up to Yahweh’s house, and all the men of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem with him, with the priests, the prophets, and all the people, both small and great; and he read in their hearing all the words of the book of the covenant which was found in Yahweh’s house.

The king stood by the pillar, and made a covenant before Yahweh, to walk after Yahweh, and to keep his commandments, his testimonies, and his statutes, with all his heart, and all his soul, to confirm the words of this covenant that were written in this book; and all the people agreed to the covenant.

The king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, and the priests of the second order, and the keepers of the threshold, to bring out of Yahweh’s temple all the vessels that were made for Baal, for the Asherah, and for all the army of the sky, and he burned them outside of Jerusalem in the fields of the Kidron, and carried their ashes to Bethel.

He got rid of the idolatrous priests, whom the kings of Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places in the cities of Judah, and in the places around Jerusalem; those also who burned incense to Baal, to the sun, and to the moon, and to the planets, and to all the army of the sky.

He brought out the Asherah from Yahweh’s house, outside of Jerusalem, to the brook Kidron, and burned it at the brook Kidron, and beat it to dust, and cast its dust on the graves of the common people.
He broke down the houses of the male shrine prostitutes that were in Yahweh’s house, where the women wove hangings for the Asherah.

He brought all the priests out of the cities of Judah, and defiled the high places where the priests had burned incense, from Geba to Beersheba; and he broke down the high places of the gates that were at the entrance of the gate of Joshua the governor of the city, which were on a man’s left hand at the gate of the city.
Nevertheless the priests of the high places didn’t come up to Yahweh’s altar in Jerusalem, but they ate unleavened bread among their brothers.
He defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.

He took away the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun, at the entrance of Yahweh’s house, by the room of Nathan Melech the officer, who was in the court; and he burned the chariots of the sun with fire.

The king broke down the altars that were on the roof of the upper room of Ahaz, which the kings of Judah had made, and the altars which Manasseh had made in the two courts of Yahweh’s house, and beat them down from there, and cast their dust into the brook Kidron.

The king defiled the high places that were before Jerusalem, which were on the right hand of the mountain of corruption, which Solomon the king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Milcom the abomination of the children of Ammon.
He broke in pieces the pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and filled their places with men’s bones.

Moreover the altar that was at Bethel, and the high place which Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin, had made, even that altar and the high place he broke down; and he burned the high place and beat it to dust, and burned the Asherah.

As Josiah turned himself, he spied the tombs that were there in the mountain; and he sent, and took the bones out of the tombs, and burned them on the altar, and defiled it, according to Yahweh’s word which the man of God proclaimed, who proclaimed these things.

Then he said, “What monument is that which I see?” The men of the city told him, “It is the tomb of the man of God, who came from Judah, and proclaimed these things that you have done against the altar of Bethel.”
He said, “Let him be! Let no one move his bones.” So they let his bones alone, with the bones of the prophet who came out of Samaria.

All the houses also of the high places that were in the cities of Samaria, which the kings of Israel had made to provoke Yahweh to anger, Josiah took away, and did to them according to all the acts that he had done in Bethel.
He killed all the priests of the high places that were there, on the altars, and burned men’s bones on them; and he returned to Jerusalem.
The king commanded all the people, saying, “Keep the Passover to Yahweh your God, as it is written in this book of the covenant.”
Surely there was not kept such a Passover from the days of the judges who judged Israel, nor in all the days of the kings of Israel, nor of the kings of Judah;
but in the eighteenth year of king Josiah, this Passover was kept to Yahweh in Jerusalem.

Moreover Josiah removed those who had familiar spirits, the wizards, and the teraphim,  and the idols, and all the abominations that were seen in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem, that he might confirm the words of the law which were written in the book that Hilkiah the priest found in Yahweh’s house.

There was no king like him before him, who turned to Yahweh with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses; and there was none like him who arose after him.
Notwithstanding, Yahweh didn’t turn from the fierceness of his great wrath, with which his anger burned against Judah, because of all the provocation with which Manasseh had provoked him.

Yahweh said, “I will also remove Judah out of my sight, as I have removed Israel, and I will cast off this city which I have chosen, even Jerusalem, and the house of which I said, ‘My name shall be there.’”
Now the rest of the acts of Josiah, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
In his days Pharaoh Necoh king of Egypt went up against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates; and king Josiah went against him; and Pharaoh Necoh killed him at Megiddo, when he had seen him.

His servants carried him in a chariot dead from Megiddo, and brought him to Jerusalem, and buried him in his own tomb. The people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah, and anointed him, and made him king in his father’s place.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign; and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, according to all that his fathers had done.
Pharaoh Necoh put him in bonds at Riblah in the land of Hamath, that he might not reign in Jerusalem; and put the land to a tribute of one hundred talents of silver, and a talent  of gold.
Pharaoh Necoh made Eliakim the son of Josiah king in the place of Josiah his father, and changed his name to Jehoiakim; but he took Jehoahaz away, and he came to Egypt and died there.

Jehoiakim gave the silver and the gold to Pharaoh; but he taxed the land to give the money according to the commandment of Pharaoh. He exacted the silver and the gold of the people of the land, from everyone according to his assessment, to give it to Pharaoh Necoh.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zebidah the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, according to all that his fathers had done.

footnotes.content: When a king discovers the law of God had been lost, his first thought is to gather the leaders—not in anger, but in calling the elders to witness what God has done. Josiah understands that repentance works best when the whole people sees the king bow first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo of Josiah in this story—a call to wholehearted repentance, to seeking God's Word when it has been lost or ignored, to tearing down the idols we've tolerated, and to remembering that faithfulness in our generation doesn't save the next one. We are each responsible for our own turning to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Picture it: king, priests, prophets, and all the people—from the least to the greatest—crowded into the temple courtyard to hear the covenant read aloud. The very public reading is the reform itself. Christ-centered families also gather around Scripture, knowing that shared hearing changes a household.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A king stands by the pillar and promises with his whole heart and soul. The covenant ceremony, so public and so sincere, shows that repentance—real turning—flows from a decision made before witnesses. We too choose to follow Jesus publicly, not in secret.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Kidron Valley becomes the furnace for false gods—Baal, Asherah, the celestial deities that had seduced kings for generations. Josiah doesn't hide or preserve the idols; he destroys them publicly and scatters their ashes at Bethel, where they were first erected. Sometimes repentance means burning the bridges behind you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those idolatrous priests had been appointed by *kings*, not by God—generations of rulers had installed them to tend the high places. Josiah's reform cuts the chain; he shows that no king's word, no matter how old, binds us to evil. The Lord's law alone matters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Asherah pole that stood in God's own house is dragged out, burned to dust in the Kidron, and scattered on the graves of common people. What an image—the false goddess given no dignity, no sanctuary, nowhere to hide. Sometimes mercy means being ruthless with idolatry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The shrine prostitutes' houses stood *inside God's temple*—sexual sin had nested itself in the very place meant for holiness. Josiah demolishes them without hesitation. We too must sometimes ask: what compromise have I allowed to settle in the rooms of my heart that should belong to the Lord alone?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Geba in the north to Beersheba in the south, Josiah removes every high place—a geographic sweep of the entire kingdom. The worship at the gate of Joshua (ancient Jebusites' old stronghold, a place name itself) shows how deep idolatry had rooted. One man's repentance can reshape a whole nation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests of the high places don't get to serve at Jerusalem's true altar—they've lost their office but not their lives. It's a mercy, but a stern one. Grace doesn't always mean restoration to the same place we were; sometimes it means learning to live in a smaller room than we'd known.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Topheth, in the Valley of Hinnom, had become the furnace where parents burned children alive to Molech—darkness had a name and a place. Josiah defiles it so thoroughly that no one can ever use it that way again. Some evils must be unmade from the earth itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Horses and chariots dedicated to the sun god stood at the temple entrance—a perversity, placing false worship at the threshold of the true house. Josiah seizes them and burns them, reclaiming the threshold itself. Small gestures sometimes carry the weight of everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rooftop altars belonged to Ahaz and Manasseh, kings who had turned their backs on God. Their stone foundations are beaten down and cast into the Kidron—no monument left standing for their rebellion. Josiah teaches us that repentance sometimes means erasing what others built, starting fresh.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon himself had built high places for Ashtoreth and Chemosh to honor his foreign wives—even a great king's wisdom couldn't make that sin wise. Josiah doesn't excuse it because it came from Solomon. The Lord's law stands above anyone's legacy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pillars and Asherah poles are broken to pieces; their places filled with the bones of the dead. Josiah uses the most defiling substance in ancient law—human remains—to make those sites forever unsuitable for worship. He's saying: this ground belongs to the Lord, and I'm consecrating it by making it unclean for idolatry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam the son of Nebat had made Israel sin centuries before—his high place at Bethel was the original wound. Josiah travels north to Bethel to demolish it himself, as if saying: no sin's roots are so old that I won't dig them up. True repentance reaches backward to heal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Josiah's spies are everywhere—even tombs become landmarks in his survey of idolatry. He orders the bones of ancient kings exhumed and burned as a fulfillment of a prophet's word spoken centuries before. He's saying: the Lord's word *will be kept*, even if it takes generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men of the city stop Josiah, pointing to one tomb: a man of God had come from Judah and warned against that very altar, centuries earlier. His prophecy had been forgotten but hadn't died. Some faithful words are spoken to an age that doesn't listen, yet they outlive their scorners.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Josiah's respect for the prophets' bones shows his faith isn't rigid—he honors those who spoke truth long ago, leaving their graves untouched. A king who will burn Baal's vessels will still revere the faithful dead. Discernment knows what to tear down and what to cherish.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Josiah doesn't stop at Judah's borders—he carries his reform into Samaria, where the northern kingdom had fallen long ago. He's restoring not just his own people but the *land itself* to God's purposes, as though healing the nation's wound.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Josiah kills the priests of the high places—a drastic measure, yet it shows that some evils demand an end without compromise. He burns men's bones on those false altars, defiling them utterly. After the reform is complete, he returns to Jerusalem bearing the weight of it all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: With the land cleansed, Josiah commands the Passover—the feast of remembrance and deliverance. It's the perfect next step: after we sweep out the idols, we gather to remember who God is and what He's done. Cleansing and remembrance belong together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not since the judges had such a Passover been kept—not even in Solomon's golden age. Josiah's reform has created a window into the way things *ought* to be, when God's people gather without compromise and remember their true King.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In Josiah's eighteenth year—not his first year, but after eighteen years of growing into his faith—he keeps this great Passover in Jerusalem. Spiritual maturity takes time; the Lord uses years to deepen a king's commitment before the greatest work begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Familiar spirits, wizards, teraphim, idols—every layer of false trust is removed. Josiah's reform doesn't stop at the temple's grand gestures; it reaches into the homes and hearts where the deepest superstitions lodged. He's protecting his people from the slow poison of compromise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No king like him before or after—Josiah holds the record for wholehearted devotion, turning with *all* his heart, *all* his soul, *all* his might, according to all Moses' law. The repetition isn't poetry; it's the truth: there is no one greater. And yet—the story's not over.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One man's repentance, no matter how sincere and thorough, cannot undo generations of his people's rebellion. The Lord's wrath, kindled by Manasseh's provocation, still burns. We are humbled: our own faithfulness doesn't erase what came before, and we can't save our nation alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even as Josiah reforms, the Lord has already set Israel's fate. Judah too will be removed from His sight as Israel was; Jerusalem will be cast off, despite the name God once put there. It's a mercy wrapped in judgment—the Lord still speaks, still warns, even when the end is set.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chronicler points us to the official record—Josiah's acts are written in the book of the kings of Judah. His story doesn't end here; it's one chapter in the long account the Lord keeps of His people's faithfulness and failure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Josiah marches against Pharaoh Necoh at Megiddo, a place of ancient battles, and falls there. His death comes not from internal rebellion but from external war—the Lord allows a righteous king to fall in battle, teaching us that faithfulness doesn't guarantee earthly victory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Josiah is brought back dead to Jerusalem and buried in his own tomb—an honor, though a grave is still a grave. His son takes the throne quickly, and the people hope for continuity. Yet sometimes the greatest king's passing marks the beginning of a nation's end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoahaz is young—twenty-three—and his mother is Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. The genealogy matters: we are watching the transition from a reformer to a son, and wondering if the son learned his father's faith or only his throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoahaz does evil, "according to all that his fathers had done." Not all of it—just the evil part. He ignores his father Josiah's example and follows the darkness of those before him. A single reformer's faithfulness can't force the next generation into righteousness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh Necoh captures Jehoahaz at Riblah and demands tribute—one hundred talents of silver, one of gold. An Egyptian king now dictates Judah's terms. The land Josiah reformed is already slipping into foreign hands, and the king who fails to defend it pays the price.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh replaces Jehoahaz with Eliakim, Josiah's other son, and renames him Jehoiakim—a vassal king with an Egyptian-approved name. Jehoahaz is taken to Egypt to die as a prisoner. In just verses, we see Josiah's reform crumble under foreign pressure and family division.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoiakim squeezes the people to pay Pharaoh's tribute, extracting silver and gold from everyone according to their assessment. Where Josiah had drawn people together for covenant, his sons now extract wealth from them for foreign masters. Repentance's fruit can spoil quickly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoiakim is twenty-five and reigns eleven years—a long reign compared to his brother's three months. His mother is Zebidah, daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah. Again, genealogies watch over the throne, marking which son rises and which falls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoiakim does evil in the Lord's sight, like his fathers before him—completing the cycle that began when idolatry nested itself in the temple. Josiah's great reform, so thorough and sincere, couldn't outlast him. Yet it remains: a king *can* turn to the Lord with all his heart, even if nations cannot be saved by one man's faith alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
